idiom_name: weakref module: ref, WeakValueDictionary, WeakKeyDictionary, WeakSet, WeakMethod, finalize (stdlib)
implementation_notes: The standard library is the realization: weakref.ref(obj) is callable and returns the object or None, WeakValueDictionary, WeakKeyDictionary and WeakSet build weak containers that drop entries when the referent dies, WeakMethod specifically supports bound methods, and weakref.finalize registers a cleanup callback that is documented to survive until the object is collected. CPython's reference counting makes absence appear promptly in the common case, but it is still not a deletion contract - cycles delay collection until the cyclic collector runs, and objects that define __slots__ without __weakref__, or built-in scalar types, cannot be weakly referenced at all. Weak containers replace the classic hand-written registry entirely; nothing needs to be unsubscribed.
pitfalls: ref(obj)() returns None and there is no way to hold the referent through the weak reference: promote once into a local (obj = ref()) and use that - a second call can already return None.

WeakValueDictionary holds keys strongly but values weakly, WeakKeyDictionary the other way round: a value that references its own key pins the entry, and entries only vanish when the weakly held side dies, so unbounded weak maps still grow between collections.
Not every object is weak-referenceable: int, str, list and instances of classes whose __slots__ omit __weakref__ raise TypeError, so a weak cache cannot use them as keys or values.

weakref.finalize callbacks must not capture the object (directly or through a bound method) or it never becomes collectable; callbacks run at most once and exceptions raised in them are printed, not propagated.
